name: Creation as ordering of pre-existing chaos
plain_explanation: Unlike the Jewish and Christian God, Plato's God does not create the world out of nothing; he finds pre-existing matter moving in a disorderly way and brings order out of that disorder, shaping it, so far as possible, to resemble an eternal, perfect pattern.
precise_definition: The Timaeus's account of the Demiurge (Creator) as a craftsman-God who, being good and without jealousy, imposes mathematical order and proportion on already-existing, chaotically moving material, modeling the resulting world as closely as possible on the eternal archetype apprehended by reason.
why_it_mattered: It commits Plato to a form of creation ex materia rather than ex nihilo, avoiding the problem of evil that troubles Christian theology (since the imperfections of the world can be blamed on the recalcitrance of pre-existing matter, not on God).
historical_origin: Distinctively Plato's own construction in the Timaeus, drawing on Pythagorean cosmology.
examples: 'Finding the whole visible sphere not at rest, but moving in an irregular and disorderly fashion, out of disorder he brought order.'
competing_positions: Jewish and Christian creation ex nihilo, which Russell notes Plato's account explicitly is not.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Avoided the problem of evil that plagues theologies committed to creation ex nihilo by a wholly good, all-powerful God.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly reshapes inherited religious creation narratives into a philosophical cosmology.
